pr_title: Allow hostnames in Access Control Lists
pr_body:
##### Summary
The Access Control List (ACL) configuration parameters can now use hostnames with simple patterns. Incoming connections are resolved using reverse DNS to obtain the hostname. Where a hostname is resolved, forward DNS resolution is performed to check the IP address is really associated with the hostname. If the checks pass then the patterns supplied are checked. Any patterns supplied for numeric ip addresses are also checked.

##### Component Name
daemon

##### Additional Information
Fixes #6438

pr_comments:
@cosmix I think that all of your comments have been addressed, please take a look at the new commits.

When you are happy with the code I can squash the commits into a single.
What did you have in the `allow connections from` field?

> What did you have in the `allow connections from` field?

```
allow connections from = localhost <hostname>
allow dashboard from = localhost <hostname>
```
Was it a connection from 127.0.0.1 that failed?

> Was it a connection from 127.0.0.1 that failed?

No, it was a connection from the external host IP that fails.
I hadn't looked at the `allow dashboard from` settings. I tested it by curling the "host:19999" part from a host with a FQDN. I'll need to change the setup of the test and get back to you.

I've setup a new test environment, firstly I tried:
```
[web]
allow connections from = localhost ua-xxx-xxx-xxx-xxx.telenor.se
```

This worked as expected, I can only connect from the host with the FQDN or via a nginx proxy running on the host. If I add the other line that you tried so that I have:

```
[web]
allow connections from = localhost ua-xxx-xxx-xxx-xxx.telenor.se
allow dashboard from = localhost ua-xxx-xxx-xxx-xxx.telenor.se
```

Then I get an error message that says "You are not allowed to access this resource.".

Does this match what you see when you test it?

> Then I get an error message that says "You are not allowed to access this resource.".
> 
> Does this match what you see when you test it?

Yes.

Well then the fix is simple, remove the extra dashboard line :)

In that particular case the check is redundant as the `allow connections from` config prevents the dashboard from being opened on any machine that does not match the pattern. I assume that you are thinking about a more sophisticated answer though, to add some functionality that was not requested in the original issue. What kind of scope do you have in mind?
One useful case would be a config like the following:
```
[web]
    allow connections from = 130.100.*.*
    allow dashboard from = projector*
```
i.e. use the dashboard config to restrict the range specified in the connections config, and the hardest case there is if the original match in the accept_socket() was numeric then handle the DNS checks later in web_client_update_acl_matches(). It is not obvious how to do that with looking around the code some more, I'll need to check how the client_ip members in the POLLJOB and the web_client related to each other and how they are used from the rest of the code. My first estimate would be to add a client_host field in the same style and use "UNKNOWN" or "UNRESOLVED" to handle the different cases and call the dns checks later if necessary. Is this roughly what you have in mind?

Yes, it does work without it. But: That the check is redundant does not mean it should result in failure. On the contrary, it should function as it would had the `dashboard` line been commented out: it should allow whoever matches both lines to connect. What is happening here is bad from a user experience perspective. A valid host cannot connect, despite being listed in both the general `allow connections from` and the more specific `dashboard` lines. Doesn't get more esoteric than this. :)

So that's not a fix.

Now, for the other case you mention — yes, that's what I had in mind and I agree that would be beyond the scope of the original request.

So, while I admit that the "let's restrict the hosts further to what's already specified in the general allow connections from line" case is something else entirely, I don't think having _the same_ hosts on dashboard and the general line should result in denied access to valid hosts, be they specified via IP or hostname (btw the with an IP it still works, even if both lines are active)

It will be a while before I check in some code to handle each of the host configuration options that are visible in ewb_client_update_acl_matches() (as I need to go through most of the web server code to see where web_client structures are used and how they relate to the POLLINFO structure in the socket code). In the meantime I found this buffer overflow that you may want to merge separately.
Thanks @amoss that's great. Could you please send the buffer overflow fix in another PR so that we can deal with it separately from this one?
New PR#6817 with just the one commit.

Gents, the check isn't redundant. "allow connections from" determines if I should permit a connection at all, even before checking what the request is about. Unless a host appears there, it doesn't matter what you put in the other allow from, it just won't connect.

Adding the hostname also to "allow dashboards from"  is one way to let that hostname access the dashboard. Another is to have * in the "allow dashboards from", so whatever is allowed from "allow connections from" will be allowed to access the dashboard. 

I haven't read the code, but my understanding is that the change was made only on the first level, which means it will need to be fixed.
@cakrit I think that much was clear to Andrew. :)

I can confirm that much was clear to me :)

I looked at the other relevant cases and I'm going to tie it together so that each of the configuration options:
```
allow dashboard from
allow registry from
allow badges from
allow management from
allow streaming from
allow netdata.conf from
```
Will work in the same way: each one allows a refinement of the set of allowed connections using a mixture of ip addresses and hostnames.

##### Question summary

I've been unsuccessful in trying to lock down the rather excellent Netdata running on a cloud VPS from a US based host via the Netdata.conf allow options. I'd greatly appreciate some assistance or perhaps improved documentation.

I want it to remain accessible on my VPS localhost if necessary but need to lock down web access to myself. The Google sign in doesn't seem to provide this since Netdata is immediately visible via the ipaddress:19999 url.

If I add my IP address to the allow connections from line in Netdata.conf, it lets me view Netdata, but my home IP is a dynamic one provided by my UK fibre broadband provider and changes occasionally or I reboot or update my router.

My router auto updates a Netgear Dynamic DNS hostname with my current IP address, so I tried using this domain in the allow connections field, but it doesn't work even though the hostname resolves to my IP address correctly. 

This works okay:

`allow connections from = localhost 86.xxx.xxx.999`

This doesn't work at all, access denied!

`allow connections from = localhost example.mynetgear.com`

Thank you.

comments: Well, netdata isn't meant to replace the need for firewalls. Without asking to verify, I expect that the reason hostnames are not allowed in the access list is to prevent query performance issues from DNS lookups. The check against the access list is executed every time a socket is opened, so the performance hit could become very significant. Implementation-wise it wouldn't be that difficult to do it, but I'm not certain it's a good idea. I may be wrong of course, let me check internally.

I discussed with @ktsaou . He's ok doing it, but it's more complex than I thought, since it's extremely easy for someone to spoof a hostname. He'd need to do the following:
- Reverse lookup on the originating IP to get a list of hostame(s) declared for that IP
- Forward DNS lookup on hostnames, to ensure the IP appears there. 
- Match one of the validated host names with the names in the access list.

We will move forward if there is sufficient interest on this from the community, so like the issue if you want it to move forward, or take a crack on implementing it!

Thank you for the informative response, much appreciated. I understand, yes probably there are much more efficient ways to reduce access. I tried the method posted this week about putting it behind Apache but it didn't work for me, I use CentOS7 not Ubuntu, so you get half way and run into errors about no such file or directory etc. 

We're encouraged as server admins not to reveal any unnecessary details about potential services and other information even in general, from the perspective of best practice and target hardening. criminals and door rattlers will look for any potential opening, so I'd like to reduce opportunity if possible. He says after posting his server and OS config!

> He says after posting his server and OS config!

ROFL!

> I tried the method posted this week about putting it behind Apache but it didn't work for me, I use CentOS7 not Ubuntu, so you get half way and run into errors about no such file or directory etc.

This will sovle you problem, apache [mod_authz_host](https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/mod_authz_host.html) is what you need.

Hello,

That is indeed a nice feature too, especially on hosts where you want to reduce all installed software (and a web server is not a small one, attack surface speaking). So to have netdata definitely standalone, that's a real gain (like on hypervisors or IoT)

Let me add my infrastructure & security experience: 
- Contrarily of forward dns where multiple hosts can point to the same IP, a reverse dns only points to 1 name. So you should only have 0 or 1 hostname for the originating IP 
- Most servers have a DNS cache (let it be sssd, nscd, local dnsmasq...) 
- many hosts don't have a reverse at all.
- we often use (or would like to) wildcard inside the name (eg:  host-*-admin.mycorp.com) or plain domain (.mycorp.com) to avoir constant configuration update.
- DNS server may protect themselves from query flood.

> since it's extremely easy for someone to spoof a hostname.

Well, it's not *that* easy to spoof dns, especially on custom / corp DNS. But I'd appreciate a recent scenario where this has been done to prove me wrong. 

That feature with the https + auth would be a lovely addition to get netdata fully standalone (dns to quickly filter out incoming request, then auth for real access filter). That avoids possible DoS by having a flood on the available web threads.
